newsitem.title: USA: Auto parts to spur magnesium surge - Hydro.
newsitem.headline: Auto parts to spur magnesium surge - Hydro.

text.p: Greater use of magnesium in auto parts will help boost consumption of the light metal by 55,000 tonnes, or 15 to 20 percent, over the next three years, Hydro Magnesium said.

Dwain Magers of Hydro Magnesium marketing told an International Magnesium Association automotive seminar late last week in Michigan that the total world market for magnesium was set to grow from 295,000 tonnes in 1996 to about 350,000 tonnes by the year 2000, and more than 500,000 tonnes by 2006.

"With announced new production capacity coming on stream from the Dead Sea Project in Israel, Noranda in Canada, Queensland Metals in Australia plus announced or anticipated expansion by existing producers, supply is expected to be kept in balance with demand during this period," Magers said in his presentation.
Hydro, part of Norway's Norsk Hydro group, produces magnesium in Norway and Canada.
Growth will be led by the use of magnesium in diecast auto parts, rising from 51,000 tonnes of parts consumed in 1996 to slightly over 100,000 tonnes in 2000, and close to 200,000 tonnes by 2006.
Auto parts which will consume more magnesium between now and 2000 are cylinder head covers, intake manifolds, instrument panels, brackets, steering columns, seats, and drivetrain components.
"This growth will be led by the North American market, followed by Europe, South America and the Pacific Rim," Magers said.
Using magnesium parts instead of aluminum or other metals, lightens the vehicle.
The investment by Volkswagen AG in the Dead Sea magnesium project has given considerable momentum to other magnesium programs in Europe, Magers added.
In the past two years some 30 diecasting machines have been bought in Europe, mainly for auto parts.

The big car companies are already lining up with magnesium producers, VW with Dead Sea, General Motors has a long-term contract with Norsk Hydro, Ford recently invested in the Queensland Metals project, and the Aisin (Toyota) Group invested in the Noranda project in Canada.
"This trend has not gone unnoticed by other major automobile producers," Magers said. "I believe we will see additional alliances being formed."
Recycling capacity is also expanding, such as Hydro's commissioning of a new 10,000 tonnes per year recycling plant in Norway.

The growth in tonnage in magnesium auto parts in Japan, however, is much smaller than in the U.S. and Europe, because the country's diecasting sector can only make small to medium sized castings, Magers said.
Korea's magnesium diecasting is still in its infancy.

After 2000, new applications for magnesium in European cars may include engine blocks, engine hood, roof panels, structural supports, rear deck lid, wheels, inner door frames, reinforcement panels and grill reinforcement, Magers said.
